The 12 Best Restaurants in New York City

Huy Vu 10/19/2026

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 19:58
Instaread

New York City has always been an attractive destination for us because of the dense crowds, diverse population, and bustling city life. This combination gives way to an incredible art scene, never-ending Broadway experiences, and, of course, endless food options from so many ethnic cuisines. From cheap eats and grab-and-go options to over 70 Michelin-starred restaurants, this city’s got you covered for food.

Now that we have family and friends who live in New York, we visit even more regularly. For context, we love to travel for food (see all our travel posts), and along with Chicago, San Francisco, and Las Vegas, NYC is one of the best dining destinations in America. From our many visits here, below is our personal list of some of the best restaurants in New York City:

1. Jungsik ($$$$), TriBeCa

If you want to experience a Michelin-star dinner but don’t want to commit to a 2-3+ hour tasting menu, then sit at the bar at Jungsik. This three-star Michelin restaurant hails from South Korea, but some say its New York location is even better at showcasing bold, contemporary Korean cuisine. When you sit at the bar counter at Jungsik, you can order à la carte from a smaller menu, so you don’t have to shell out the $335 per person tasting menu. The best part is that you get to pick from a list of their best hits. Yes, the items are still pricey, but if you want a lighter, quicker meal to try a few items, this is a good option that’s not normally offered at places with tasting menus. 

We picked the banchan course ($35) for each person, and they recommended ordering one for each person because each dish is one bite. The banchan presentation highlighted Jungsik’s modernist twist. Where traditional Korean restaurants showcased each dish in metal or plastic bowls, Jungsik’s banchan were bite-sized pieces of art placed on stark white platforms, like artwork on museum pedestals. My favorites were the marinated raw shrimp (Saewoo Jang), soft silken tofu (Yun-dubu), and raw seasoned beef (Yukhwe) bites. 

And we also split the sea urchin bibimbap ($80). What a very luxurious dish. If you love uni, you’ll definitely need to order this entree. This bibimbap showcases a whole layer of uni on top of plump seaweed rice, pungent kimchi, and crispy quinoa. Once mixed, every bite felt perfectly balanced with sweet, salty, and vinegary flavors.  

What left the biggest impression on us, though, was the extremely cool staff. The staff here seem to expertly combine professionalism with charm and kindness. From the hosts to the servers and beyond, we left with full bellies and grins. Jungsik is a great last-night-in-NYC dinner for great memories. 

Type of food: Korean contemporary
Price: $$$$ ($300 pp)
What to order: banchan, sea urchin bibimbap
Address: 2 Harrison St, New York, NY 10013 (TriBeCa)
Website | Yelp

2. Dashi Okume ($$), Greenpoint

Dashi Okume was originally on our radar for their custom dashi mixes; however, we ended up staying for their traditional Japanese breakfast platters and shopping options. It’s the first place we’ve visited since our Japan trip, where the rice was cooked into perfectly plump, tender short-grain rice. This meal was super simple, but it made me reminisce about our amazing breakfasts at Hotel Mitsui in Kyoto. 

We ordered two breakfast platters and chose the protein (Saikyo-Zuke and Yakijake), side dish, and drink. My favorite was the miso-marinated Japanese blue fish because it was sweet, savory, and buttery. The trays also come with a side of pickles made for the day, miso soup with in-house-made broth, and rice. They also have beer for additional purchase if you need a mid-day pick-me-up. 

And once you’re done, you can shop around the different Japanese stores inside the building, make your own dashi mix, or sample different versions to take home as souvenirs. We’ll definitely be coming back on future trips. 

Type of food: Japanese
Price: $$ ($45 pp)
What to order: breakfast platter, dashi  
Address: 50 Norman Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11222, USA
Website | Yelp

3. Naks ($$$), East Village

Trying new Filipino restaurants is always on our to-do list, like Donia from London or Kasama in Chicago, so Naks was a necessary stop on our NYC trip. Naks offers Filipino and Filipino American comfort foods in a contemporary style, and Chef Eric Valdez named the restaurant after a Tagalog expression to mean “delight.” With this dinner menu, I was definitely wowed and delighted. 

We started with the tangy, creamy kinilaw made from tuna cured in a broth of coconut vinegar, radish broth, and ginger oil. This was an elevated kinilaw from what I grew up with, but it’s just as refreshing and light. My favorite of the night was the lechon platter that feeds at least two people (but easily four!) and has the crispiest roasted lechon belly I’ve had in a while. It comes with garlicky jasmine rice and a side of veggies. 

If you like cocktails, pick one of their seasonal drinks featuring island flavors like calamansi, ube, pandan, and more. They also offer non-alcoholic beverages that are just as tasty. Naks is popular, so make a reservation before your trip to get a table. 

Type of food: Filipino American 
Price: $$$ ($50 pp)
What to order: Lechon platter, kinilaw 
Address: 201 1st Ave, New York, NY 10003, USA (East Village)
Website | Yelp

4. Mr_Himm__ ($$), Harlem

Don’t skip Instagram food spots because I’ve had some of the best home-cooked, affordable, and well-seasoned food from cottage chefs I’ve found on the Internet. While I was visiting family, a cousin followed Mr_Himm__ on Instagram, saw he was offering seafood pick-ups during our stay, and placed an order. We’re no strangers to doing our own seafood boils with crawfish, blue crab and dungeness crab, but ordering pre-made crab is always a treat.

Mr_Himm__ from Harlem offers delicious cajun seafood for very affordable prices. You order through his Instagram and pick up at a nearby shop called A Taste of Seafood in Harlem. We ended up ordering a dozen crabs for about $40 – an insanely good deal if you ask me. We easily split this between four people. The crabs came in a steaming container and were very thoroughly seasoned. 

For someone who grew up on Vietnamese Cajun seafood, this seasoning is most similar to that with loads of paprika, garlic, onion, butter, and cayenne. It was a full flavor bomb. The crabs were a good size, had a lot of meat for blue crabs, and the meat was super sweet and tender. 

He also offers snow crabs, shrimp, mussels, seafood salad, and empanadas. If you love cajun-style seafood, you’ll love ordering from Mr_Himm__ and I definitely plan on getting more crabs the next time I’m in Harlem. 

Type of food: seafood, blue crabs 
Price: $$ ($50 pp)
What to order: blue crabs 
Address: 2 W 125th St, New York, NY 10027 (Harlem)
Website 

5. Omakase by Korami ($$$), Hell’s Kitchen

Omakase by Korami is an intimate dinner with only 10 bar seats and offers a very reasonable omakase experience: $89 per person for 15 courses. If you’ve been to other similar experiences before, you’ll understand how this is a deal. Our friend had previously eaten here and took us because she was impressed with the fresh selections. 

Our only critique was being unintentionally charged for an extra course we never asked for: an eel handroll at the end. We were confused when we saw the check and further requested more details. The staff realized this was a mistake on their end and refunded us the incorrect charges (after they confirmed via video evidence of the # of dishes served to us), but it was an odd situation to deal with once we got home. 

15 courses were more than enough to fill our bellies–too much if you ask me. The fish ships from Japan daily, and they offer a variety of options year-round. The rice on each nigiri was perfectly cooked, tender, but still plump and unbroken, and the seasoning was tangy and well-balanced. My favorites of the night were the uni with sweet shrimp (super umami and sweet) and the red snapper, slightly torched for an extra smoky flavor. In addition to the original courses, you can also add supplemental dishes, like toro negi or caviar. Along with omakase, they also had a selection of sake and beers. I chose a yuzu sake cocktail that tasted very refreshing in between bites of nigiri. 

Type of food: Japanese, omakase 
Price: $$$ ($89 pp)
What to order: omakase 
Address: 400A W 50th St, New York, NY 10019 (Hell’s Kitchen) 
Website | Yelp

6. Bánh by Lauren ($), Chinatown

I’ve followed Bánh by Lauren on Instagram and watched her open up a brick-and-mortar after lots of pop-ups, and I finally got to try out her bánh bò (Vietnamese honeycomb cake) the last time we went to New York. Coming from SoCal, where plenty of old-school Vietnamese bakeries sell bánh bò, I was eager to try a different variety from a first-gen baker, especially since I know how finicky this dessert can be to make. 

Lauren’s honeycomb cake uses the familiar pandan extract (which I was super happy to learn was natural, not artificial!), and it had a chewy, mochi-like center with a soft crust. It hit that good level of “not-too-sweet” flavor that many Asians agree is the proper sweetness level. Compared to old-school bakeries, each slice is definitely pricier ($5 per slice). 

We also tried her Thai tea chiffon cake, which had a light, fluffy texture with hints of bold tea and a nutty coconut-whipped-cream frosting. She also sells this chiffon cake in flavors like pandan and Vietnamese coffee. You can enjoy your pastries inside Bánh by Lauren, but there are few seats; however, there are some patio seats too.   

Type of food: Vietnamese American bakery, pastries 
Price: $ ($20 pp)
What to order: pandan honeycomb cake, chiffon cake, cute merch
Address: 42 Market St, New York, NY 10002
Website | Yelp

7. PopUp Bagels ($), Midtown West

Bagels are a hot topic in New York City, and there are endless bagel shops to visit with a hefty following of fans. One of our favorite shops is PopUp Bagels, which was down the street from our hotel. PopUp Bagels has five locations in Manhattan, and we visited the Midtown West location multiple times during our week-long stay for breakfast, with a line outside every time. Even in 50-degree weather, we waited patiently for piping-hot, straight-out-of-the-oven bagels with savory cream cheese schmears. 

PopUp Bagels’ menu lets you order a fixed number of bagels (3, 6, or 12), and each order comes with a small tub of cream cheese of your choice. The menu is simple: they make traditional bagel flavors (poppy, salted, sesame, everything, and plain) and a variety of schmears, including a couple of daily options like spinach artichoke or tomato basil cream cheese. 

My top favorite from PopUp Bagels was the everything bagel dipped right into their spinach artichoke cream cheese. The ultra-soft centers and crunchy edges of the bagels are the perfect vehicle to scoop out the cheese. I would describe myself as indifferent to bagels most of the time, but PopUp Bagels are just too delicious not to love. 

Type of food: bagels and cream cheese
Price: $ ($15 pp)
What to order: any fresh bagel, scallion cream cheese, daily cream cheese flavor 
Address: 177 Thompson St, New York, NY 10012 (Midtown West)
Website | Yelp

8. La Cabra ($), SoHo and East Village

La Cabra was the best coffee shop I’ve visited on multiple trips to New York City. It’s shocking that such a dense and popular food destination doesn’t have more specialty, 3rd wave coffee. Hailing from Denmark, La Cabra is one of Europe’s most respected specialty coffee roasters. We’re lucky that one of our local shops in Orange County often stocks La Cabra, and we’ve brewed it at home often through their online coffee bean subscription.

My order is a medium/light roast hot oat milk cortado or flat white, in a ceramic cup–this combination is almost impossible to come by in NYC. Hot coffee in a paper cup is a dealbreaker (for health reasons, and this rules out over 85% of shops), and the rest tend to serve dark roasts. 

But luckily Manhattan has two locations for La Cabra, one in East Village and one in SoHo, only about ¾ of a mile from each other. The coffee was excellent, and I don’t take that for granted. It’s a bonus that both locations have beautifully designed minimalist interiors. Both locations have a large display case of pastries, but if I’m being honest, they were just ok. I’d never visit just for the pastries, but hands down La Cabra is a must-visit for me until better shops pop up and make it into our rotation. There is also a further location in Bushwick where they roast coffee beans, and you can also order drinks. 

Type of food: cafe and pastries
Price: $ ($8 pp)
What to order: oat cortado
Address: 284 Lafayette St, New York, NY 10012 (SoHo) or 152 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003 (East Village Bakery)
Website | Yelp

9. Kora ($$), Sunnyside

Filipino American bakeries are having a moment in the food sphere right now, from Kasama in Chicago to 61Hundred Bread in Orange County. And in New York, there’s Kora. This bakery originally started out as a donut pop-up and quickly grew in popularity–I even know someone whose Kora donuts were stolen at a bar post-pick-up (truly tragic). Now we’re so glad they have a brick-and-mortar location in Sunnyside. It was a bit of a trek to get to Kora if you’re staying in Manhattan, but it is worth it! 

Growing up in both the US and the Philippines, I had my fair share of ensaymada because my dad loved eating it, but I didn’t like the (too often) dried-out brioche, overly sweetened cream, and shredded cheese topping. However, Kora’s ensaymada croissant changed my mind. Its flaky, rich croissant paired perfectly with the slightly pungent Eden cheese topping and sweet butter spread. 

Kora also offers a full coffee bar with traditional espresso drinks and fusion lattes like pandan, hojicha, and ube. When we first arrived, there was a short line, but it moved quickly, and they bake fresh pastries throughout the day. 

Type of food: Filipino American bakery, pastries 
Price: $$ ($20 pp)
What to order: ensaymada croissant, salted egg babka swirl 
Address: 45-12 Greenpoint Ave, Sunnyside, NY 11104
Website | Yelp

10. Korkscrew Bistro ($$), Bedford Stuyvesant

Sometimes unplanned dinners and impromptu searches for nearby spots are the best way to find really good local meals. This is how our large group of 8 ended up at Korkscrew Bistro in Bedford on a busy Saturday night. 

Korkscrew Bistro is a local wine-and-beer bistro with American-Italian dishes we’re all familiar with, but it hits the spot when you’re hungry and don’t know where to go. We were surprised Korkscrew Bistro could seat our group comfortably, but luckily, they had a larger back area with large tables and more privacy. The staff guided us on dish suggestions in a pretty nonchalant way, and we definitely overordered. I would say their portions were similar to The Cheesecake Factory, where you can assume any order will need a takeout box.

We ended up ordering multiple kale Caesar salads, truffle fries, and lamb ragu with pappardelle. Each dish came in mountain servings. The kale Caesar was very fresh, bright, and well dressed. Each bite was fresh, with massaged kale, shaved Brussels sprouts, and plenty of shaved parm on top. If I see truffle fries on the menu, I will order them no doubt. And Korckscrew Bistro’s truffle fries might be some of my favorites. They were extra crispy and golden, coated with earthy truffle sauce and, again, a mountain of shaved parm. Lastly, the lamb ragu pappardelle was rich and meaty, especially with a dollop of ricotta on top of thick, handmade pasta cooked perfectly al dente. 

Korkscrew Bistro offers a full wine, beer, and bar menu, plus non-alcoholic options. We were fully satisfied after our hearty plates of pasta, salads, appetizers, and drinks. 

Type of food: American Italian, wine & beer bistro 
Price: $$ ($50 pp)
What to order: kale Caesar salad, truffle fries, lamb ragu pappardelle 
Address: 165 Tompkins Ave, New York, NY 11206 (Bedford Stuyvesant)
Website | Yelp

11. Daniel Corpuz Chocolatier ($), Chinatown

For a sweet treat or if you’re in need of souvenirs, check out Daniel Corpuz Chocolatier. This shop focuses on Filipino-Asian-inspired truffles, chocolates, and other treats. Daniel Corpuz Chocolatier is tucked away in Chinatown with a few tables and a small team making fresh treats in-house. 

Daniel helped our group choose flavors since it was our first time. My favorites were caramelized banana (turon), ube, calamansi, and roasted corn. Each was a burst of flavor. The turon had bits of crispy caramel pieces to offset the silky filling. I liked the contrast between tangy citrus and rich chocolate in the calamansi, too. The roasted corn was a new take on truffles, offering a sweet-and-savory option. These truffles are about the size of a nickel but have lots of flavor; we ordered an assortment and still managed to split each truffle among five of us. Daniel also mentioned that during the holidays, they offer special flavors like tonka vanilla and chestnut truffles. 

Type of food: truffles, chocolate, dessert 
Price: $ ($15 pp)
What to order: calamansi truffles, roasted corn truffles, caramelized banana truffles
Address: 60 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013 (Chinatown)
Website | Yelp

12. 54 Below ($$), Theater District

If you’re an avid Broadway fan, you’ll want to visit 54 Below. This underground theater has hosted many Broadway legends and rising stars. Think of 54 Below as a supper club that features live singing and shows that any die-hard theater fan would love to experience. I first found 54 Below YouTube videos a decade ago and have wanted to experience it in person ever since.

I snagged a late-night ticket for their ongoing “54 Broadway’s Greatest Hits” show at 9:30 P.M. This show features songs from legendary musicals like CATS, Chicago, and more. Seating is included, and pricing depends on the seating type. Large booths line the back of the dining room, side barstools line the counter, and four-tops sit in the center of the room in front of the stage. Ticket prices depend on where you sit; we chose a side bar counter since there were only three of us. It does get a bit cozy, but that’s all part of the live show and ambiance. 

There is a full bar and dinner menu to choose from, and each ticket includes a $25 food-and-drink minimum per guest. Since we had a late show, we had a smaller menu, but it still offered a full meal. I chose their seasonal cocktail flight that came with a special green Grinch-themed cocktail margarita, white wine spritzer, bourbon peach sour, and a Cosmo-inspired cocktail. They were very liquor-forward and slightly too sweet for me, but my group enjoyed them. As usual, I also ordered French fries that were a nice, quiet snack to eat during the show. 

I wouldn’t come here just for the food, but the show is exceptional. If you want an intimate live show and amazing singers, definitely go see a show at 54 Below. There are plenty to choose from many, many different songbooks. 

Type of food: American 
Price: $$ ($50 pp)
What to order: cocktail flight if you like alcohol forward drinks
Address: 254 W 54th St, New York, NY 10019 (Theater District) 
Website | Yelp
